title: Why Familiarity Breeds Liking
summary: Discover the mere exposure effect, a psychological phenomenon where people develop a preference for things simply because they are familiar with them.
evidenceNote: While widely demonstrated across various stimuli, research also shows that excessive exposure can lead to an inverted-U shape where liking eventually declines into wear-out or ad fatigue.

scenes.text: Why do you start to like a song only after hearing it a few times?
Known as the mere-exposure effect, it's a psychological phenomenon where familiarity breeds preference.
Newly hatched chicks preferred the tone that was played to them while they were still in the egg.
Robert Zajonc found that affective reactions like liking can happen with minimal stimulus input, even without conscious awareness.
A 2017 meta-analysis pooled this many findings from 81 articles on repeated exposure.
Too much repetition can backfire into an inverted-U shape, leading to wear-out or ad fatigue.
Simply put: we often grow to like things just because we see them more often.

sources.title: A re-examination of the mere exposure effect: The influence of repeated exposure on recognition, familiarity, and liking
